explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says John "…sent his disciples" to ask Jesus his question (Matthew 11:2-3). From inside a prison he can't go himself, so his own people carry it for him. No phone, no group chat, just good friends with good legs.

I see why a centurion might come to mind, but he's not in this passage at all. The text says John sent his disciples. They're the ones who went to Jesus with the question. So the messengers are John's own people, not a soldier.

Good guess, baker, but this passage never mentions a steward. It only says John heard about the works of Christ in prison and sent his disciples. They're the ones carrying the question, which makes this a very short list of messengers. No steward needed.

explanations.answer: If Jesus is the One who was to come
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the question. The disciples ask Him, "Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?" It's a direct question, and I love that it gets asked out loud. Jesus doesn't brush it off, and we'll see what He sends back.

explanations.answer: If Jesus will come to the prison
explanations.explanation: Nope, nobody asks about a visit. The question is about who Jesus is: "Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?" It's a question about His identity, not His travel plans. Nobody's asking Him to drop by with a cookie box, either.

explanations.answer: If Jesus will pray for him
explanations.explanation: Praying is a good thing to ask for, but it's not what John asks here. His disciples bring one question to Jesus: "Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?" That's all about who Jesus is. The text doesn't mention a prayer request.

True! Jesus lists it right in the report: "…the dead are raised…" That's in the middle of the list, not at the end. It sits right between the deaf hearing and the good news going to the poor, like it's one more item. It's quite a list, baker.

It's actually true, so this one slipped past you. The report Jesus sends includes this line: "…the dead are raised…" It's right there in the list of what John's disciples will hear and see. Easy one to miss when the list keeps going.
Yes, poor! Jesus finishes the report with "…the good news is preached to the poor." It's the last item on the list. I wish I'd had that kind of news in the back of my drawer.

Ooh, I see the thinking, baker, but rich never made it onto this list. Rich tried to sneak in like a raisin in the chocolate chip batch, and the list wasn't having it. Jesus ends His report with "…the good news is preached to…" and the word after that isn't rich. That's the last thing He tells John's disciples to carry back.

Priests are a fair guess, since they show up all over the Bible, but not in this list. Jesus says "…the good news is preached to the poor." It's the closing item in His report to John. So the word that fits is poor.

explanations.answer: Whoever doesn't fall away because of Him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, "Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me." That's how He wraps up His answer to John, who asked his question from prison. I think that's a tender thing to say to a man sitting in a cell. The blessing is for the one who does not fall away.

explanations.answer: Whoever gives up everything for Him
explanations.explanation: That sounds big and brave, but it isn't what Jesus says here. His words are "Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me." So the blessing is for the one who does not fall away on account of Him. Stick with the exact words.

explanations.answer: Whoever keeps watch through the night
explanations.explanation: Keeping watch through the night is a good habit, but it isn't what Jesus says here. His closing words to John are "Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me." Nobody's pulling an all-nighter in this verse. The blessing goes to the one who does not fall away.

That's right. Jesus says, "Look, those who wear fine clothing are found in kings’ palaces." Palaces are the place He names for fine clothing. He's asking the crowds what they went out to see, and I love how He walks them through it.

Close to the right neighborhood, but that's not what Jesus says. He says, "Look, those who wear fine clothing are found in kings’ palaces." The temple courts don't come up in that line. The place He names is a palace.

City gates would be a busy spot to see people, but Jesus doesn't mention them here. He says, "Look, those who wear fine clothing are found in kings’ palaces." So the answer is palaces. Jesus asks the crowds what they went out into the wilderness to see, and palaces are the place He names for fine clothing.

Close, but Jesus says more than that. He asks, "A prophet?" and then answers, "Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet." Yes, John is a prophet, but that isn't all Jesus says about him. It's the "and more" that makes this one false.
Right! Jesus doesn't stop at prophet. He says, "Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet." He said yes to the question, then added something bigger. That's why "nothing more" is false.

Yes, prepare! Jesus quotes the words: "Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You." That's the job of the messenger, and Jesus says it's John. I know a little something about preparing, baker, because my ovens never stop.

Guarding is a real job, but it's not the one in this verse. Jesus quotes, "Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You." The messenger goes ahead to prepare the way. That's the word you're looking for.

Nice thought, but light isn't the word. The verse says, "Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You." Jesus says that's about John. He's the one sent to prepare the way.

True! Jesus says, "Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has risen no one greater than John the Baptist." He opens with "Truly I tell you…" so you know He means it. Nobody born of women has risen greater than John, which is a high compliment.

That one's actually true, baker. Jesus says, "Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has risen no one greater than John the Baptist." He says it plainly, with no "but" in that part of the sentence. The "yet" comes after it, and we'll get to it next.

explanations.answer: The least in the kingdom of heaven
explanations.explanation: Yes! Jesus says, "Yet even the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he." He's just said that no one born of women has risen greater than John. Then the "yet" lands, and it's the least in the kingdom of heaven. That one made me stop and think.

The disciples are a fair guess, but Jesus doesn't name them here. He says, "Yet even the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he." Nobody gets picked out by name. The answer is the least in the kingdom of heaven.

explanations.answer: The prophets who came before him
explanations.explanation: Not quite. In this passage Jesus says, "For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John." But the one He calls greater than John is "…even the least in the kingdom of heaven…" He never puts the earlier prophets in that spot.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "And if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who was to come." He says it plainly. It comes with an "…if you are willing…" so He leaves it to the crowd to take it in.
Reasonable guess, baker, but Isaiah isn't the name Jesus gives here. He says, "…he is the Elijah who was to come." So the name in this verse is Elijah.

Jeremiah's a fair guess, but Jesus doesn't name him in this passage. He says, "…he is the Elijah who was to come." Elijah is the name on the card. I'd have taken a guess like yours, baker, but this time the answer is Elijah.

Yes, children. Jesus says this generation is "…like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling out to others…" It's a picture of kids who want the others to join in. The comparison is simple, and Jesus uses it on purpose to make a point.

A marketplace full of merchants makes sense, and it's an easy guess to make. But Jesus says the ones sitting there are "…children sitting in the marketplaces and calling out to others…" The merchants don't make it into the picture. It's kids who are calling out.

Jesus doesn't mention soldiers in this picture. He says they're "…children sitting in the marketplaces and calling out to others…" Picture kids calling out to others. Soldiers aren't part of what Jesus describes, so the answer is children.

That's right. Jesus says, "For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon!’" That's a hard thing to say about anybody. I think it must have stung to have people say that about John.

That's not what the text says they said. Jesus says, "For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon!’" The words are about a demon, not a false prophet. That's the line people use against John here.

The text doesn't say they called John proud. Jesus says, "For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon!’" That's the accusation, plain and sharp. Pride never comes up in this passage.

Not this time. Jesus, the Son of Man, came eating and drinking, and they say, "Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!" So they still find something to say, and it isn't approval. Different way of coming, same story: they still have a complaint.

Right, false. Jesus says the Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, "Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!" John came one way and got one complaint, and Jesus came the other way and got a different complaint. Nobody was handing out gold stars.
